title: Accessibility First, Not Last
intro: Watching an AAC app give his non-verbal son a voice led Calabro to a rule he's used since 2015: usability is largely a subset of accessibility.

learn.title: Before the app
learn.text:
Asking for juice could mean twenty minutes of wrong guesses, with Seth getting more frustrated at each one.

The LAMP communication app changed that — and changed how Calabro works. Since 2015 he errs on the side of accessibility best practice, while noting the rare cases where it conflicts with usability guidance.

try.q: What rule did the experience give him?
options: Usability is largely a subset of accessibility
Accessibility and usability are separate disciplines
Assistive technology should be tested separately
Accessibility matters most in public-sector products
try.explain: So optimise for accessibility and everyone benefits.

learn.title: Two starting points
learn.text:
**Aesthetics first:** beauty is decided, usability is layered on, the accessible version hides in Settings, and users with impairments fix it themselves — often finding it still fails the basics afterwards.

**Accessibility first:** constraints are set before the visuals, the product is accessible by default, and no burden is shifted to the user.

try.q: What is the core question Calabro asks of Apple's Liquid Glass?
options: Why wasn't the accessible version the default?
Why wasn't it tested with more users?
Why does it need so much GPU power?
Why was it announced before it was finished?

learn.title: No excuses at either end
learn.text:
He had already argued that scrappy startups can't use “no time” as a reason to skip accessibility.

If that doesn't hold for them, it certainly doesn't hold for the world's largest design teams.

*Context: the critique was written at the June 2025 announcement and Apple has adjusted the design since. The principle doesn't date.*

try.q: Who does the “no time for accessibility” excuse apply to, in his view?
options: Only teams without a design system
try.explain: If a startup can't use it, neither can a company with Apple's resources.

learn.title: Where to spend the effort
learn.text:
In the WebAIM screen reader survey (#9, 2021), about **68%** navigate a long page by **headings first**. Landmarks are first for only about 3%. About **90%** use a screen reader on a **phone**.

Audit in five layers: **automated, keyboard, screen reader, visual and a full task flow.**

The survey is from 2021. Check for a newer edition before quoting.

try.q: How do most screen-reader users scan a long page first?

test.q: What does AAC technology do in this story?
options: Gives a non-verbal child a way to communicate
Magnifies the screen for low vision
test.explain: The LAMP app replaced twenty minutes of guessing.

test.q: Since when has Calabro applied this rule?
test.explain: Nine years into his UX career.

test.q: What does “accessible by default” mean in practice?
options: The accessible configuration ships as the standard one
Accessibility settings are easy to find
The product passes an automated audit
test.explain: Not an option the user has to go and switch on.

test.q: What is the burden the article objects to?
options: Users with impairments adjusting every control
test.explain: The people least able to carry it end up carrying it.

test.q: Does Calabro say accessibility and usability guidance never conflict?
options: He says the conflicts are frequent
He says usability should win when they clash
test.explain: He errs toward accessibility while acknowledging the rare contradictions.

test.q: Roughly how many screen-reader users also use one on a mobile device?
test.explain: Test on a phone, not only on desktop.

test.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five audit layers?
test.explain: The five are automated, keyboard, screen reader, visual and flow.
